L15: cite9†View PDF cite10†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:In this paper, we address the issue of hyperspectral pan-sharpening, which consists in fusing a (low spatial resolution) hyperspectral image HX and a (high spatial resolution) panchromatic image P to obtain a high spatial resolution hyperspectral image. The problem is addressed under a variational convex constrained formulation. The objective favors high resolution spectral bands with level lines parallel to those of the panchromatic image.
L17: This term is balanced with a total variation term as regularizer. Fit-to-P data and fit-to-HX data constraints are effectively considered as mathematical constraints, which depend on the statistics of the data noise measurements. The developed Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) optimization scheme enables us to solve this problem efficiently despite the non differentiabilities and the huge number of unknowns.

In: Proceedings of Whispers 2014, pp. 1-4. IEEE Xplore. WHISPERS 2014, 2014-06-24 - 2014-06-27, Lausanne, Switzerland. doi: cite11†10.1109/WHISPERS.2014.8077507†doi.org . Full text not available from this repository.Official URL: cite12†http://core.ieee-whispers.com/†core.ieee-whispers.com L10: ## Abstract
L11: This paper introduces the new scheme of the previously proposed Joinly Sparse Fusion of Hyperspectral and Multispectral Imagery (J-SparseFI-HM) fusion method. This extended, now fully automated and parallelized version of J-SparseFI-HM jointly estimates bundles of an adjustable number of high resolution hyperspectral bands by fusing corresponding low resolution bands with possibly multiple high resolution multispectral ones.
L12: Which multispectral bands are individually used is decided via a decision matrix that is calculated from the spectral response functions of the multispectral sensor. Tests are performed on the SuperMUC petascale system. Recently acquired 0.75 m airborne VNIR HySpex data is used to synthesize a WorldView-2 image as well as low resolution hyperspectral data with a down-sampling factor of 10.
L13: The fusion results are compared to those produced by three state-of-the-are hyperspectral resolution enhancement methods.

L28: Chanussot. Super-resolution of hyperspectral images using local spectral unmixing. IEEE ABSTRACT For many remote sensing applications it is preferable to have images with both high spectral and spatial resolutions. On this regards, hyperspectral and multispectral images have complementary characteristics in terms of spectral and spatial resolutions.
L29: In this paper we propose an approach for the fusion of low spatial resolution hyperspectral images with high spatial resolution multispectral images in order to obtain super-resolution (spatial and spectral) hyperspectral images. The proposed approach is based on the assumption that, since both hyperspectral and multispectral images acquired on the same scene, the corresponding endmembers should be the same.
L30: On a first step the hyperspectral image is spectrally down-sampled in order to match the multispectral one. Then an endmember extraction algorithm is performed on the down-sampled hyperspectral image and the successive abundance estimation is performed on the multispectral one. Finally, the extracted endmembers are up-sampled back to the original hyperspectral space and then used to reconstruct the super-resolution hyperspectral image according to the abundances obtained from the multispectral image.

L169: 1. INTRODUCTION
L170: 
L171: Many efforts have been spent in the last decades to improve
L172: the spectral and spatial resolutions of remote sensing sensors.
L173: 
L174: However, there are design constraints that result in an in-
L175: 
L176: verse relation between spatial and spectral resolution. More-
L177: 
L178: over, the system trade-off related to data volume and signal-
L179: 
L180: to-noise ratio (SNR) limitations prevent to achieve both of
L181: 
L182: them simultaneously. Many practical applications require im-

L184: ages having both high spectral and spatial resolution. Thus,
L185: 
L186: there is a need for techniques that fuse high spectral resolution
L187: images, such as hyperspectral images (HS), with high spatial
L188: 
L189: images such as multispectral images (MS) or panchromatic
L190: 
L191: images (PAN), in order to obtain high spectral and spatial

L193: (super-resolution) images. In the literature there exist many

L125: ABSTRACT
L126: 
L127: For many remote sensing applications it is preferable to have
L128: 
L129: images with both high spectral and spatial resolutions. On this
L130: 
L131: regards, hyperspectral and multispectral images have comple-
L132: 
L133: mentary characteristics in terms of spectral and spatial reso-
L134: 
L135: lutions. In this paper we propose an approach for the fusion
L136: 
L137: of low spatial resolution hyperspectral images with high spa-
L138: tial resolution multispectral images in order to obtain super-
L139: 
L140: resolution (spatial and spectral) hyperspectral images. The
L141: 
L142: proposed approach is based on the assumption that, since both
L143: 
L144: hyperspectral and multispectral images acquired on the same
L145: 
L146: scene, the corresponding endmembers should be the same.
L147: 
L148: On a ﬁrst step the hyperspectral image is spectrally down-
L149: 
L150: sampled in order to match the multispectral one. Then an
L151: 
L152: endmember extraction algorithm is performed on the down-
L153: sampled hyperspectral image and the successive abundance
L154: 
L155: estimation is performed on the multispectral one. Finally, the
L156: 
L157: extracted endmembers are up-sampled back to the original
L158: 
L159: hyperspectral space and then used to reconstruct the super-
L160: 
L161: resolution hyperspectral image according to the abundances
L162: 
L163: obtained from the multispectral image.
L164: 
L165: Index Terms—hyperspectral imaging, super-resolution,
L166: 
L167: spectral unmixing.

L169: 1. INTRODUCTION
L170: 
L171: Many efforts have been spent in the last decades to improve
L172: the spectral and spatial resolutions of remote sensing sensors.
L173: 
L174: However, there are design constraints that result in an in-
L175: 
L176: verse relation between spatial and spectral resolution. More-
L177: 
L178: over, the system trade-off related to data volume and signal-
L179: 
L180: to-noise ratio (SNR) limitations prevent to achieve both of
L181: 
L182: them simultaneously. Many practical applications require im-
L183: 
L184: ages having both high spectral and spatial resolution. Thus,
L185: 
L186: there is a need for techniques that fuse high spectral resolution
L187: images, such as hyperspectral images (HS), with high spatial
L188: 
L189: images such as multispectral images (MS) or panchromatic
L190: 
L191: images (PAN), in order to obtain high spectral and spatial
L192: 
L193: (super-resolution) images. In the literature there exist many
L194: 
L195: applications combining hyperspectral and panchromatic im-
L196: 
L197: ages [1]. These techniques, that goes under the name of pan-
L198: 
L199: sharpening, are considered adequate when applied to multi-
L200: 
L201: spectral and PAN images, but have many drawbacks when the
L202: low-resolution image is a hyperspectral image [2]. Recently,
L203: 
L204: some techniques dedicated to the fusion of hyperspectral im-
L205: 
L206: ages and multispectral ones have been proposed [3][4][5]. In
L207: 
L208: general, the approach is to associate the fusion problem with
L209: 
L210: linear spectral unmixing, which assumes that the underlying
L211: 
L212: data can be described by a mixture of a relatively small num-
L213: 
L214: ber of pure spectral signatures, corresponding to the materials
L215: 
L216: present in the scene. Since both hyperspectral and multispec-
L217: tral images capture the same scene, the endmembers should
L218: 
L219: be the same. Therefore, the spectral information extracted
L220: 
L221: from one of the images should also be able to explain the
L222: 
L223: other one. Due to the high spectral resolution of a hyperspec-
L224: 
L225: tral image, the endmembers can be extracted from this data,
L226: 
L227: and then used to reconstruct the multispectral image. Since
L228: 
L229: the multispectral image have high spatial resolution, the ﬁ-
L230: 
L231: nal reconstructed image will be at super-resolution. In [4] the
L232: same approach has been followed with the only difference
L233: 
L234: that the mixing matrix is replaced by a dictionary learnt using
L235: 
L236: a non-negative matrix factorization with sparsity regulariza-
L237: 
L238: tion on the code. In [5], the hyperspectral data is unmixed
L239: 
L240: via the K-SVD algorithm, and the multispectral data is recon-
L241: 
L242: structed using orthogonal matching pursuit to induce sparsity.
L243: 
L244: In [6] alternately unmixes both sources of data to ﬁnd the sig-
L245: 
L246: natures and the abundances of the endmembers, while in [3]
L247: two dictionaries were learned from the two different data, and
L248: 
L249: then used a dictionary-pair learning method to establish the
L250: 
L251: correspondence between them.
L252: 
L253: However, the effectiveness of these approaches strongly de-
L254: 
L255: pends on how the dictionaries can be obtained. In this pa-
L256: 
L257: per we propose an approach where the endmembers are ex-
L258: 
L259: tracted directly from the spectrally down-sampled hyperspec-
L260: 
L261: tral image. The derived endmembers are used as input to an
L262: unmixing algorithm applied to the multispectral image. The
L263: 
L264: obtained abundances are then used to reconstruct the super-
L265: 
L266: resolution hyperspectral image. This approach permits to re-
L267: 
L268: duce the spectral distortion of the enhanced image. The re-
L269: 
L270: mainder of the paper is organized as follows: in Sec. 2 the
L271: 
L272: proposed super-resolution methodology is introduced and in
L273: 
L274: Sec. 4 experimental results are presented. Finally in Sec. 5
L275: 
L276: conclusion remarks are provided.

L414: 3. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

L417: real datasets. The super-resolution images obtained in both

L423: Mapper (SAM) quality indexes. ERGAS and SAM will both

L425: produce positive values with an ideal value of 0. However,

L427: values that are around 3 are referred to a good image enhance-

L429: ment. SAM is a useful measure of the spectral quality in-

L432: spectral and spatial quality. A qualitative analysis, through

L434: visual inspection, will also be discussed.

L607: 4. CONCLUSIONS
L608: 
L609: In this paper we have presented an approach for the super-
L610: 
L611: resolution of hyperspectral images by fusing them with mul-
L612: 
L613: tispectral images. Since both hyperspectral and multispectral
L614: 
L615: images capture the same scene, they should also be able to de-
L616: tect the same endmembers with different spectral resolutions.
L617: 
L618: Based on this assumption, spectrally downsample hyperspec-
L619: 
L620: tral endmembers should then correspond to the multispectral
L621: 
L622: endmembers. In this work NFINDR was used to extract a
L623: 
L624: set of endmembers from the Spectrally downsample hyper-
L625: 
L626: spectral image while the abundance are obtained by solving
L627: 
L628: a constrained least squares problem applied to the multispec-
L629: 
L630: tral image. In order to improve the quality of super-resolution
L631: images and also to avoid that the number of endmembers may
L632: 
L633: be higher than the number of spectral bands , we proposed a
L634: 
L635: local approach, where the images are partitioned into patches
L636: 
L637: and the method is applied independently on each patch. Ex-
L638: 
L639: periments on two real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness
L640: 
L641: of the proposed approach to produce super resolution hyper-
L642: 
L643: spectral images with low spectral distortion and spatially con-
L644: 
L645: sistent.
